result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of Laconia, describing shrines, springs and places around Therapne, Mount Taygetus, Helus and the road to Arcadia. He records local lore: the origin of the Helots, Tyndareus' oath over the horse, and Icarius' statue of Modesty.

scenes.title: Therapne, Alesiae and Pharis
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists fountains and shrines near Therapne, the origin of mills at Alesiae, and the shrine of Messapian Zeus near Pharis.

scenes.title: Mount Taygetus
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Bryseae, the summit Taletum, the hunting grounds, and the Eleusinian temple of Demeter with its Orpheus statue.

scenes.title: Helus and the Helots
scenes.summary: Helus is described, with its founding by Heleus and its fall to the Dorians, which gave the Helots their name. Nearby sites on Taygetus follow.

scenes.title: Road to Arcadia
scenes.summary: Along the road to Arcadia stand the temple of Achilles, the tomb of the Horse where Tyndareus bound Helen's suitors by oath, and seven pillars.

scenes.title: Icarius and Penelope
scenes.summary: Icarius pleads with Penelope to stay in Lacedaemon, but she veils her face and he lets her go, setting up a statue of Modesty.
scenes.stakes: Icarius risks losing his daughter to distant Ithaca.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable origin story for a statue of Modesty, from Penelope's silent veiling.

analysis.text: Pausanias links places to myths and cults, showing how landscape preserved local memory.
The account of Helus explains the Spartan Helots, whose servitude was central to Spartan society.

legacy.text: Pausanias' etymology of Helot from Helus was long repeated, though it is now debated.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes that the Persians also sacrifice horses to the Sun, comparing Spartan and Persian cult.

language_notes.text: Enyalius is a war-god title, here an epithet of Ares; the Spartan youths sacrificed to him before fighting-style contests.
"Earth-holder" translates a Poseidon epithet meaning he holds or supports the earth, linked to earthquakes.
Alesiae is explained by Pausanias from the Greek verb for grinding; "Mill-town" gives the supposed etymology.
A hero-chapel (heroon) is a shrine for a deified mortal, honored with offerings rather than as a full god.
The comparison with Persians refers to their well-known worship of the Sun and sacrifice of horses to it.
Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis, is said to have come here; the reference to her wanderings is assumed known.
Hercules' wound refers to his fight with Hippocoon's sons at Sparta; Æsculapius is the healing god.
Orphic rites were mystic ceremonies attributed to the legendary singer Orpheus, concerned with purification and the afterlife.
Quoted from the Catalogue of Ships in Homer's Iliad (Book 2), which lists the Greek contingents sent against Troy.
Helots were the state-owned serfs of Sparta, who worked the land; Pausanias derives the name from Helus.
Pausanias compares the Helots' name to Hellenes, said to derive from the small region Hellas in Thessaly, a name extended to all Greeks.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 180-200 metres.
Tyndareus, Helen's father, bound her suitors by oath so they would defend whoever became her husband; this later led to the Trojan expedition.
The seven planets meant the seven wandering heavenly bodies known to the ancients: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
Odysseus is called Ulysses in some translations; this one uses Odysseus here, and Penelope is his wife of Homer's Odyssey.

context_notes.text: Therapne, southeast of Sparta, was a cult center of the Dioscuri and Menelaus and Helen.
Castor and Polydeuces (Pollux) were the twin sons of Leda, especially honored at Sparta.
Dionysus' cult often had restricted rites; women-only worship was typical of his rituals.
Demeter was goddess of grain and of the Eleusinian Mysteries, so this Laconian temple borrows the Attic cult's title.
The Dorians were the Greek people who came to dominate the Peloponnese, including Sparta, in the traditional account of the Dorian invasion.
Platanistas was a plane-tree grove near Sparta where youths fought ritual battles in teams.
Neoptolemus was Achilles' son, so Prax descended from Achilles' line, explaining the Spartan temple to Achilles.
Icarius was Penelope's father, brother of Tyndareus, and was associated with Sparta.

literary_notes.text: "They say" shows Pausanias distancing himself from local tradition, reporting rather than vouching for it.
The piling up of "excellent," "superfine" hunting of every beast gives a lively, almost boastful tone unusual in Pausanias' plain survey.
The oath over the horse's entrails anticipates the later war at Troy, when the suitors must honour it.
Icarius' pursuit of the chariot shows a father's deep attachment and sets up Penelope's quiet, devoted character.
Penelope's veil becomes a silent sign of her choice and of her modest virtue, which the statue commemorates.
